intro: To add a new layer in Photoshop on Mac, go to Layer > New > Layer or press ⇧⌘N. The new layer appears above the layer you have selected in the Layers panel.
tldr: Press ⇧⌘N to open the New Layer dialog, name the layer, and click OK.
Prefer the menu? Choose Layer > New > Layer. It does the same thing.
Press ⇧⌥⌘N to add a layer straight away, with a generic name and no dialog.
Press ⌘J to copy the current layer or selection onto a new layer.
Command-click the New Layer icon in the Layers panel to place a layer below the selected one.

blocks.text: A layer is a separate sheet inside a Photoshop file. Each layer holds its own pixels, text, or shape, and the layers stack on top of each other. That stack is what lets you change a shadow without touching the logo, or swap a background without redoing the type. New layers come up all the time, so the shortcut is worth learning once and keeping. This page covers the Photoshop desktop app on a Mac. It walks through the menu, the keys, the Layers panel, and the fixes for the problems that stop people most.
Add a layer with the Layer menu

Start by clicking the layer you want the new one to sit above. In the Layers panel, click the layer name, not the eye icon. Then go to Layer > New > Layer. Photoshop opens the New Layer dialog. Type a name, then click OK. The new layer appears above the selected layer, so the stack reads the way you expect.

Naming is worth the few seconds it takes. A name like Logo shadow tells you what the layer does. A generic name tells you nothing once the file grows. Future you will thank present you when the file gets reopened after a week away from the project.
Use the ⇧⌘N shortcut for a named layer

Press Shift, Command, and N together. The same New Layer dialog opens. This is the fastest way to add a named layer, because your hands stay on the keyboard. It helps when you are painting, moving a shape, or typing a caption. The shortcut needs an open document. A layer lives inside a file, so Photoshop needs a file to put it in.
Skip the dialog with ⇧⌥⌘N

Press Shift, Option, Command, and N together to add a layer with no dialog. Photoshop gives it a generic name and drops it into the Layers panel. Use this when you are sketching fast and the names do not matter yet. You can still rename the layer later from the Layers panel. Pick the key combination that matches the job, not the one you remember best.
Copy a layer or selection with ⌘J

Command+J works differently. It copies the current layer or the current selection onto a new layer. Use it when you want a duplicate of a photo cutout, a shape, or a part of a layer you have already selected. The copy is a new layer. The original stays where it was, so nothing you built is lost. If you want an empty layer, use ⇧⌘N or ⇧⌥⌘N instead.

blocks.text: Place a new layer below the selected one

Sometimes the new layer belongs under the one you are working on. A shadow or a paper texture is a common example. Select the layer that should sit above the new one. Then hold Command and click the New Layer icon at the bottom of the Layers panel. The new layer lands below the selected layer. Without Command, the same icon adds a layer above, as usual.

blocks.title: Background layer blocks the new layer
blocks.text: A Background layer cannot have layers placed below it. Double-click it and choose Layer from Background before you try again.
Convert a Background layer so you can add layers under it

A Background layer sits at the bottom of the stack, and Photoshop will not place a layer beneath it. You need to convert it first. Double-click the Background layer in the Layers panel. In the dialog that opens, choose Layer from Background. The layer becomes a normal layer. You can now move it, change its opacity, and place layers below it.
Adobe's layers help page describes this same route. It does not give a Mac keyboard shortcut for the conversion, so use the double-click.
Find the Layers panel when it is hidden

If the shortcut runs and you see no new layer, the Layers panel may be hidden. Open it with Window > Layers. The panel should appear on screen. If it still does not show, go to Window > Workspace and choose Essentials. Some guides say F7 shows the panel. Sources disagree about the F7 key on Mac keyboards, so use the Window menu first.
Mistakes people make when they add layers

items: Selecting the wrong layer first. The new layer appears above whatever is selected, so select the target before you add.
Pressing ⌘J when you wanted an empty layer. Command+J copies the current layer or selection, so the content comes with it.
Trying to put a layer under a Background layer without converting it first.
Leaving every layer with a generic name. Name layers in the dialog when the file will be reopened or shared.
Following an old shortcut list without checking it. The Mac shortcuts on this page come from a tutorial written for Photoshop CS6, so check the Layer menu on your copy.

blocks.text: Check the Photoshop version and macOS before you search for menus

Menu labels and shortcuts can change between releases, so check your version first. The current desktop release reported in October 2026 is Photoshop 27.11. CGChannel lists Windows 10 and macOS 14.0 or later as its compatibility, so the minimum macOS version for this release is 14.0. If your Mac runs an older system, you may not be able to install this release. To see your own version, read [how to check your Photoshop version](/how-to/check-your-photoshop-version-in-photoshop).
Adding a layer in Photoshop on the web

Adobe says Photoshop is available on desktop, web, and mobile. It also says there is no free version on the web. This page covers the Mac desktop app only. The layer menu and shortcuts on the web app were not verified for this page, so do not assume the keys above work there.

blocks.title: Check Adobe for the latest menu names
blocks.text: Adobe's own help pages could not be checked for this page. Confirm the menu names against Adobe's help for your release before you rely on them.
Worked example: a shadow under a logo

Say your logo sits on its own layer, and you want a soft shadow beneath it. Click the logo layer in the Layers panel. Command-click the New Layer icon, so the new layer lands below the logo. Name it Shadow if you plan to edit it later. Paint or fill the shadow on that layer. The logo stays on top and keeps its own settings.
If the logo sits on a Background layer, convert it first. Otherwise Photoshop will not place the shadow beneath it. This check saves a retry, and it is the most common snag in this kind of job.
What to check after you add a layer

items: The new layer name appears in the Layers panel, in the spot you expected.
The layer sits above or below the layer you selected, as you intended.
The layer is a normal layer, not a locked Background layer.
Your original layer still has its content. Command+J leaves the original in place.

blocks.text: Practice the layer keys on a blank file

Open a new document in Photoshop. Press ⇧⌘N, name a layer, and click OK. Press ⇧⌥⌘N to add a second layer with no dialog. Select a shape or a part of the first layer, then press ⌘J. A few quick passes like this show you where each layer lands. After that, the keys stop feeling like a memory test.

Once the layer is in place, you usually want something on it. For that, see [how to add text in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/add-text-in-photoshop). If the whole file needs a new size first, see [how to change canvas size in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/change-canvas-size-in-photoshop).

blocks.title: Keep the layer names readable
blocks.text: Rename a layer as soon as its job is clear. Short names like Shadow, Logo, or Texture save time when you come back later.

faq.question: What is the keyboard shortcut for a new layer in Photoshop on Mac?
faq.answer: Press ⇧⌘N, which is Shift, Command, and N. It opens the New Layer dialog so you can name the layer. For a layer with no dialog, press ⇧⌥⌘N.

faq.question: Why did my new layer appear in the wrong place?
faq.answer: Photoshop puts the new layer above the selected layer. Select the layer you want underneath before you add. If it landed in the wrong spot, use Edit > Undo and try again.

faq.question: How do I add a layer below another layer on Mac?
faq.answer: Select the layer that should sit above. Hold Command and click the New Layer icon at the bottom of the Layers panel. The new layer lands below the selection.

faq.question: Can I add a layer under the Background layer?
faq.answer: Not until you convert it. Double-click the Background layer, then choose Layer from Background. The layer becomes a normal layer that you can move and place layers beneath.

faq.question: What is the difference between a new layer and Command+J?
faq.answer: A new layer is empty. Command+J copies the current layer or the current selection onto a new layer, so the content comes with it.

faq.question: The Layers panel is gone. What do I do?
faq.answer: Go to Window > Layers. If it still does not show, go to Window > Workspace and choose Essentials. Try the menu first, then test the F7 key if you want a shortcut.

faq.question: Does the same shortcut work in Photoshop on the web?
faq.answer: This was not verified. Adobe says there is no free version of Photoshop on the web, but the web layer menu and shortcuts were not checked for this page.

faq.question: Which Photoshop version are these steps for?
faq.answer: Photoshop 27.11, the desktop release reported in October 2026. CGChannel lists macOS 14.0 or later as its requirement, so check your Mac before you install.

steps.name: Select the layer below your new layer
steps.text: In the Layers panel, click the layer name that should sit under the new one. Photoshop uses the selected layer to decide where the new layer goes. Click the name, not the eye icon, which only shows or hides the layer.
steps.tip: A selected layer is highlighted in the Layers panel.

steps.name: Open the New Layer dialog
steps.text: Go to Layer > New > Layer. Or press ⇧⌘N with the document window active. Either route opens the New Layer dialog where you can name the layer.
steps.tip: Press the three keys together, not one after another.

steps.name: Name the layer
steps.text: Type a name in the dialog. Adobe's help pages were not available for checking, so confirm the other fields, such as mode, opacity, and clipping mask, on your version.

steps.name: Click OK
steps.text: Click OK. The dialog closes and the new layer is added to the Layers panel above the selected layer.

steps.name: Check where the layer landed
steps.text: Look at the Layers panel. The new layer should sit above the layer you selected in the first step. If the panel is hidden, open it from Window > Layers, then check again.
steps.tip: If the layer landed in the wrong place, use Edit > Undo and try again.

steps.name: Add a layer without the dialog
steps.text: For a fast layer with no dialog, press ⇧⌥⌘N. Photoshop adds the layer with a generic name. Rename it later in the Layers panel.

steps.name: Place a layer below the selected one
steps.text: Select the layer that should sit above. Hold Command and click the New Layer icon at the bottom of the Layers panel. The new layer lands below the selected layer.

troubleshooting.fix: Click inside the document window so Photoshop is the active app, then press the keys again. A layer needs an open document to live in.
Go to Window > Layers. If it still does not appear, go to Window > Workspace and choose Essentials. Sources disagree on F7, so use the menu first.

troubleshooting.problem: I cannot place a layer below the bottom layer
troubleshooting.fix: The bottom layer is probably a Background layer. Double-click it in the Layers panel, then choose Layer from Background.

troubleshooting.problem: The new layer landed in the wrong place
troubleshooting.fix: Use Edit > Undo, select the correct layer in the Layers panel, and add the layer again.

troubleshooting.problem: Panels or menus still look wrong after all of that
troubleshooting.fix: Reset preferences as a last resort. Hold ⌘⌥⇧ while launching Photoshop, then confirm Yes to delete settings. Back up custom panel setups first. See [how to reset preferences in Photoshop on Mac](/how-to/reset-preferences-in-photoshop).
